Write a model in lavaan, Mplus or formula syntax

Source: R/ctModelSyntax.R
ctModelSyntax.Rd

ctModelLavaan, ctModelMplus and ctModelFormula create the same model object as ctModel, from lavaan style syntax, Mplus style syntax, or R formulas in the style of brms. ctModelSyntax writes an existing model in any of the three styles.

Usage

ctModelSyntax(model, style = c("lavaan", "mplus", "formula"))

ctModelLavaan(
  syntax,
  type = "ct",
  id = "id",
  time = "time",
  manifesttype = NULL,
  ...
)

ctModelMplus(
  syntax,
  type = "ct",
  id = "id",
  time = "time",
  manifesttype = NULL,
  ...
)

ctModelFormula(
  ...,
  type = "ct",
  id = "id",
  time = "time",
  manifesttype = NULL,
  family = NULL
)

Arguments

model

A model from ctModel or one of the functions here, or a fit.

style

'lavaan', 'mplus' or 'formula'.

syntax

Character string containing the model.

type

'ct' for a continuous time model, 'dt' for discrete time.

id

Name of the subject id column, or several names for nested levels, innermost first, as in ctModel.

time

Name of the time column.

manifesttype

Types of the indicators that are not Gaussian, as a named vector such as c(y3 = 'binary', y4 = 'ordinal'). Types are 'continuous', 'binary', 'ordinal', 'count' and 'censored', or the numbers 0 to 4 that ctModel uses. An unnamed vector with one entry per indicator is also accepted. Ordinal indicators need ncategories, and censored ones censormin or censormax, each as a named vector.

...

For ctModelFormula, the formulas, followed by any named arguments for ctModel. For ctModelLavaan and ctModelMplus, named arguments for ctModel. Useful ones are ncategories, censormin, censormax, TIpredNames, tipredDefault, PARS and driftScaled. latentNames, manifestNames and TDpredNames set the order of the variables. The model matrices themselves are written by the syntax.

family

For ctModelFormula, a brms style alternative to manifesttype. Either one family for every indicator or a named list, given as a name, a function or a family object. gaussian, bernoulli, cumulative and poisson are recognised.

Value

ctModelLavaan, ctModelMplus and ctModelFormula return a model of class ctStanModel, as ctModel does. ctModelSyntax returns the code that creates the model, as a character string that prints as code. Settings that a model holds beside its matrices, such as covmattransform, are written as assignments after the model is created. A warning says so if the code does not create the same model.

Details

What is estimated by default. Loadings, effects between processes and predictor effects are in the model only if they are written. The rest follows ctModel:

  • the first indicator of each process has a loading of 1, and other loadings that are written are free;

  • each process has a free auto effect, free noise variance and free initial mean and variance, the initial mean varies between subjects, and the noise and initial states of different processes are correlated;

  • each indicator has a free residual variance and a free intercept, and the intercept varies between subjects;

  • process intercepts are zero, and residuals of different indicators are uncorrelated.

Fix or free any of these with the statements below.

What the statements mean. An effect between processes is an entry of the drift matrix. With type = 'ct' it is the effect of one process on the rate of change of another, and with type = 'dt' the effect on its value at the next occasion. A time dependent predictor acts as an impulse, shifting the process at each occasion by the effect times the value of the predictor. A covariance that is not written, or is fixed to zero, is zero in the fitted model. Processes and indicators need different names. ctModel lets a process take the name of its indicator, but here a statement such as y1 ~ 1 would then not say which of the two it is about.

lavaan style.


eta1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3        # eta1 is measured by y1, y2, y3
eta1 ~ eta1 + a*eta2 + x    # effects on eta1: auto, cross (labelled a), predictor x
eta1 ~ 1                    # free process intercept
eta1 ~~ 0*eta2              # no noise covariance
y1 ~~ y2                    # residual covariance
y1 ~ 0*1                    # intercept fixed to zero
y4 | t1 + t2                # y4 is ordinal with three categories
a ~ age                     # age predicts the parameter a
a ~~ a                      # a varies between subjects

A number before * fixes a parameter, a name labels it, and NA frees it. Two parameters with the same label are equal, as are labels joined by ==. A label on the first indicator of a process leaves its loading at 1, and NA*y1 + a*y1 frees and labels it (y1* (a) in Mplus style). A variable on the right of ~ that is not a process is a time dependent predictor. level: 2 or level: between starts a block in which an indicator's name stands for its intercept and a process's name for its intercept, so that y1 ~ age and y1 ~~ 0*y1 there are about the intercept of y1. With nested ids, name the level, as in level: school.

Mplus style.


eta1 BY y1 y2 y3;
eta1 ON eta1 eta2 (a);      ! label a
eta1 ON x;
[eta1];                     ! free process intercept
eta1 WITH eta2@0;
y1 WITH y2;
[y1@0];
[y4$1 y4$2];                ! y4 is ordinal with three categories
s | eta2 ON eta1;           ! s varies between subjects
%BETWEEN%
s ON age;
y1@0;                       ! the intercept of y1 does not vary

@ fixes a parameter, * frees it, and a name in parentheses labels the parameters before it on the same line. In a discrete time model an effect may be written with its lag, eta1 ON eta1&1. A continuous time model has no lag, and one is refused there, because the value of a lagged effect is on another scale. If the text has sections, only MODEL: is read. With nested ids use %BETWEEN school%.

Formula style.


ctModelFormula(
  y1 + y2 + y3 ~ eta1,                 # measurement
  d(eta1) ~ eta1 + eta2 + x,           # dynamics of eta1
  d(eta2) ~ 1 + eta2 + (1 | id),       # with an intercept that varies
  drift_eta1_eta2 ~ age + (1 | id),    # a formula for one parameter
  mm_y1 ~ s(age) + (0 | id))

A formula with d() on the left gives the effects on a process. Its intercept is zero unless 1 is written. Other formulas with a variable on the left give the processes that the variable measures. A formula with a parameter name on the left describes that parameter: 1 estimates it, a number fixes it, predictors on the right are time independent predictors, s() is a smooth effect and (1 | id) makes it vary. (0 | id) stops it varying. Random effect terms may also be written in the other formulas, where (1 + eta2 | id) lets the intercept and the effect of eta2 vary. Fix or label a term with 0.5*eta2, "a"*eta2 or NA*eta1.

Parameter names. Every parameter has a name, whether it is free or fixed. The name is your label if you gave one, and otherwise a default name made from the matrix and the variables. For processes eta1 and eta2, indicators y1 and y2 and a time dependent predictor x, the default names are:

drift_eta1auto effect of eta1
drift_eta1_eta2effect of eta2 on eta1
td_eta1_xeffect of x on eta1
cint_eta1intercept of eta1
diff_eta1noise sd of eta1
diff_eta2_eta1noise covariance of eta1 and eta2
T0m_eta1initial mean of eta1
T0var_eta1initial sd of eta1
T0var_eta2_eta1initial covariance of eta1 and eta2
lambda_y2_eta1loading of y2 on eta1
mm_y1intercept of y1
mvary1residual sd of y1
mvary2_y1residual covariance of y1 and y2

print(model) shows the names of the free parameters.

A statement with a parameter's name on the left is about that parameter. This is how the styles reach the initial state, and random effects and predictors of any parameter. For the initial mean of eta1, in lavaan style:


T0m_eta1 ~ 0*1          # fix it at 0
T0m_eta1 ~ start*1      # give it the label start
start ~~ start          # it varies between subjects
start ~~ 0*start        # it is the same for every subject
start ~ age             # it depends on age

In Mplus style these are [T0m_eta1@0];, [T0m_eta1] (start);, start;, start@0; and start ON age;. In formula style they are T0m_eta1 ~ 0, T0m_eta1 ~ "start"*1, start ~ (1 | id), start ~ (0 | id) and start ~ age. The default name can be used in place of the label, and the statements can come in any order. A value given to a parameter by name is on the scale ctsem uses for that cell, which for a variance is a standard deviation. Values given with ~~, WITH or a variance statement are variances. A name that is close to a parameter name and matches none is taken as a misspelling and refused.

Other ctsem features. Wherever a label can be written, a quoted ctsem cell or a ctPar call can be written instead, such as ctPar("a", transform = "exp(param)", sdscale = 0.5)*eta2 in lavaan and formula style, or eta1 ON eta2 (a|exp(param)); in Mplus style. This gives transforms, prior scales, stated population means and state dependent expressions. The result is an ordinary model, so model$pars, ctModelMatrices, ctModelHigherOrder and the other model functions apply to it. Some things belong elsewhere. Start values are given to ctFit as inits, and priors with priors = TRUE. A stationary initial state is stationary = TRUE in ctFit. Groups are compared with a time independent predictor. Random effects are correlated with each other. poprank and popblocks in ctFit give their covariance a factor structure, and poprank = 0 with popunique = TRUE makes them independent. Higher order lags are added with ctModelHigherOrder.

See also

ctModel, ctPar, ctFit

Examples

# The same model four ways
m1 <- ctModel(LAMBDA = diag(2), manifestNames = c('y1', 'y2'),
  latentNames = c('eta1', 'eta2'), silent = TRUE)

m2 <- ctModelLavaan('
  eta1 =~ y1
  eta2 =~ y2
  eta1 ~ eta1 + eta2
  eta2 ~ eta1 + eta2')

m3 <- ctModelMplus('
  eta1 BY y1;
  eta2 BY y2;
  eta1 eta2 ON eta1 eta2;')

m4 <- ctModelFormula(
  y1 ~ eta1,
  y2 ~ eta2,
  d(eta1) ~ eta1 + eta2,
  d(eta2) ~ eta1 + eta2)

# A cross effect that varies between subjects and depends on age
m5 <- ctModelLavaan('
  eta1 =~ y1
  eta2 =~ y2
  eta1 ~ eta1 + a*eta2
  eta2 ~ eta2
  a ~ age
  a ~~ a')

ctModelSyntax(m5, 'mplus')
ctModelSyntax(m5, 'formula')
